ch01.anchor: a history of the Central Special Branch begins with stage magic
ch01.note: The Central Special Branch (Zhongyang Teke) was the Chinese Communist Party’s first professional intelligence and security service, set up in Shanghai in 1927–28 under Zhou Enlai and active until 1935. Divided into sections for general affairs, intelligence, action (the “Red Squad”), and radio communications, it shielded the Party’s underground leadership, planted agents inside the Kuomintang police and secret services, punished traitors, and built the Party’s first clandestine wireless network. Western scholarship (Frederic Wakeman, Policing Shanghai, 1927–1937) treats it as the seed of all later Chinese Communist intelligence work.

ch01.anchor: He was Gu Shunzhang.
ch01.note: Gu Shunzhang (1903–1935), a Shanghai labor organizer who commanded the workers’ pickets in the armed uprising of 1927, trained in political security in the Soviet Union, and was chosen by Zhou Enlai to head the Central Special Branch. A gifted amateur magician, he used stage conjuring as cover. Arrested by the Kuomintang in Wuhan in April 1931—recognized, it is said, while performing—he defected at once and betrayed the Shanghai underground, forcing a wholesale evacuation of the Party’s leaders; in reprisal the Special Branch killed members of his family. He was executed by the Kuomintang in 1935. His defection is the hinge of this book. (Corroborated: Wakeman, Policing Shanghai; Chinese and English reference works.)

ch01.anchor: "Let those above favor a thing, and those below will carry it further."
ch01.note: A saying from the Mencius (“Teng Wen Gong,” part I): where those above have a preference, those below will have it to a still greater degree. The author uses it to explain how the Empress Dowager Cixi’s taste for Western magic spread the fashion downward.

ch01.anchor: the favor of the Western Empress Dowager
ch01.note: The Empress Dowager Cixi (1835–1908), called the “Western Empress Dowager” (Xitaihou) after the palace she occupied, was the effective ruler of China through the last half-century of the Qing dynasty. “The last years of the Guangxu reign” are the first decade of the 1900s.

ch01.anchor: the rapid-fire patter of the *guankou*
ch01.note: Guankou is the unbroken, tongue-twisting “patter” of xiangsheng (“crosstalk”), the paired comic dialogue central to northern Chinese variety art; Ma Sanli (1914–2003) was its most celebrated modern master. Wuqiao county, in Cangzhou (Hebei), is the traditional cradle of Chinese acrobatics and conjuring, and “Ghost-Hand” Wang Baohe (1944–2016) a famous latter-day sleight-of-hand performer there. The titles in quotation marks are traditional set pieces of magic and patter.

ch01.anchor: Ruan Lingyu, the tragic queen of the silent era
ch01.note: Ruan Lingyu (1910–1935), one of the great stars of the Chinese silent screen, famed for tragic roles; her suicide at twenty-four, hounded by scandal, became a national sensation. “Butterfly Wu” is Hu Die (1908–1989), the other reigning film queen of the age. Zhang Daimin, named here, was Ruan’s common-law husband, whose lawsuits against her helped drive her to her death.

ch01.anchor: the embroiderings of Frederic Wakeman
ch01.note: Frederic E. Wakeman Jr. (1937–2006), Chinese name Wei Feide, was a leading American historian of China; his Policing Shanghai, 1927–1937 (1995) and Spymaster: Dai Li and the Chinese Secret Service (2003) are standard works on the intelligence world of this book. The author lists him (with a 2011 date, apparently a Chinese edition) among writers he thinks have inflated Gu Shunzhang’s reputation as a magician.

ch01.anchor: Zhang Guotao, 1991
ch01.note: Zhang Guotao (1897–1979) was a founder of the Chinese Communist Party and one of its most senior leaders until, having lost his power struggle with Mao, he defected to the Kuomintang in 1938; he died in Canada. His memoir, My Recollections, is much cited and much distrusted.

ch01.anchor: keeps clear of the melon patch and the plum tree
ch01.note: A classical caution (guatian lixia): one does not stoop to tie a shoe in a melon patch, nor reach up to one’s hat under a plum tree, lest one be taken for a thief—that is, one avoids even the appearance of wrongdoing.

ch01.anchor: that was Yu Zecheng.
ch01.note: Yu Zecheng is the fictional Communist mole at the center of Lurk (Qianfu), a hugely popular 2009 Chinese television spy drama; his peasant “wife” and the mercenary informer Xie Ruolin, both invoked later in this chapter, are characters from it too. The author sets a line of screen dialogue beside a maxim commonly attributed to Lenin, “the enemy never sleeps.”

ch01.anchor: The Central Special Branch had another man of resource: Chen Geng.
ch01.note: Chen Geng (1903–1961) was among the most storied figures of the Chinese Communist movement: a graduate of the first class of the Whampoa Military Academy who, during the Eastern Expeditions of 1925, personally carried his stricken commandant Chiang Kai-shek to safety. Under the alias Wang Yong he ran the intelligence (Second) Section of the Central Special Branch from 1928 to 1931. He went on to become one of the People’s Liberation Army’s ablest generals, commanded the celebrated 386th Brigade against Japan, advised the Viet Minh in 1950, and served as a deputy chief of the general staff. Much of what follows draws on his posthumously published diary and autobiography.

ch01.anchor: At the Nanchang rupture I went to Wuhan
ch01.note: The source reads “the Nanchang rupture” (Nanchang jielie). Chronologically Chen Geng reached Wuhan in the spring of 1927, before the August Nanchang Uprising named just below; the phrase seems to telescope the collapse of the Kuomintang–Communist united front that year. Rendered as printed.

ch01.anchor: the Whampoa Military Academy
ch01.note: The Whampoa (Huangpu) Military Academy, founded near Guangzhou in 1924 under the first Kuomintang–Communist alliance—Chiang Kai-shek as commandant, Zhou Enlai heading its political department—trained the officer corps of both parties. Its “first class” produced a remarkable roll of commanders who would later face one another across the civil war.

ch01.anchor: the Shakee massacre
ch01.note: On 23 June 1925, during the Canton–Hong Kong strike, foreign troops on Shamian (Shakee) island fired on a Chinese demonstration in Guangzhou, killing more than fifty—one of the touchstone atrocities of the anti-imperialist movement. The Canton–Hong Kong general strike it fed (1925–26) was the largest China had yet seen.

ch01.anchor: After the split between the Kuomintang and the Communists I joined the Nanchang Uprising.
ch01.note: The Nanchang Uprising of 1 August 1927—the Communists’ first armed revolt after the Kuomintang turned on them—is reckoned the founding day of the Red Army, later the People’s Liberation Army. Its forces were beaten within weeks and scattered south through Huichang and the Chaozhou–Shantou region, as Chen Geng’s account describes.

ch01.anchor: Xu Enzeng — in his time chief
ch01.note: Xu Enzeng (1898–1985) ran the Kuomintang’s civilian secret service, the Central Bureau of Investigation and Statistics (Zhongtong), through the 1930s. A U.S.-trained engineer and a kinsman of the Chen brothers, he was the unwitting employer of Qian Zhuangfei—the Communist mole in his own office whose warning, after Gu Shunzhang’s 1931 defection, saved the Party’s Shanghai leadership.

ch01.anchor: Dong Jianwu was a Chinese Communist agent
ch01.note: Dong Jianwu (1891–1970), the “Red Pastor,” was an ordained Anglican clergyman and Communist agent who used St. Peter’s Church in Shanghai as a safe house and meeting place. In 1936 he escorted Mao Zedong’s two young sons abroad, and he helped arrange the American journalist Edgar Snow’s journey to the Communist base. Persecuted in the Cultural Revolution, he was rehabilitated after his death.

ch01.anchor: through the ten years of turmoil
ch01.note: “The ten years of turmoil” is the standard Chinese phrase for the Cultural Revolution (1966–76), during which many veteran Communists—especially those with pre-1949 underground or foreign connections—were persecuted as suspected traitors or spies.

ch01.anchor: "Of the two ranks one soldier left, shouldering his spear, wandering alone."
ch01.note: From Lu Xun’s quatrain inscribed on his story collection Panghuang (Wandering, 1926): “A lonely new garden of letters, a quiet old battlefield; / of the space between, one soldier left, shouldering his spear, wandering alone.” The source text prints “of the two ranks” (liang zhen) where Lu Xun wrote “of the space between” (liang jian); rendered here as printed.

ch01.anchor: when Yang Du's widow came under attack
ch01.note: Yang Du (1875–1931) was among the most brilliant and mercurial figures of the early Republic: a monarchist theorist who led the Chou’an Society in urging Yuan Shikai to take the throne in 1915. Disgraced when that failed, he turned leftward and—as Zhou Enlai revealed only in 1975—secretly joined the Chinese Communist Party in his last years, passing intelligence from within Du Yuesheng’s circle. The secret-membership claim rests on Zhou’s own testimony and Party records.

ch01.anchor: threw himself into the effort to save Li Dazhao
ch01.note: Li Dazhao (1889–1927), head librarian of Peking University and, with Chen Duxiu, co-founder of the Chinese Communist Party; he led its northern organization until the warlord Zhang Zuolin had him seized from the Soviet embassy and hanged in April 1927—one of the Party’s foundational martyrdoms.

ch01.anchor: the Shanghai "notable" Du Yuesheng
ch01.note: Du Yuesheng (1888–1951), paramount boss of Shanghai’s Green Gang, was at once opium magnate, financier, philanthropist, and political fixer. He had helped Chiang Kai-shek massacre the Communists in April 1927; yet his web of connections made his household a prize for Communist intelligence, as here.

ch01.anchor: Some say Yang Du joined the Party
ch01.note: Pan Hannian (1906–1977) succeeded Chen Geng in the Party’s intelligence work and became its foremost spymaster of the 1930s and 1940s. In 1955 he was secretly arrested and, in a notorious miscarriage of justice, imprisoned for “counter-revolution” over a wartime meeting with Wang Jingwei; he died in disgrace and was posthumously cleared in 1982. His fall pulled down many he had run, including Mei Gongbin.

ch01.anchor: Pan Hannian brought Shen Duanxian — Xia Yan
ch01.note: Xia Yan (1900–1995), pen name of Shen Duanxian, was a leading left-wing playwright and screenwriter, later a senior cultural official, and in these years an underground Party member active in Shanghai intelligence and the film world.

ch01.anchor: The man who introduced Chen Geng to Yang Du was Hu Egong.
ch01.note: Hu Egong (1884–1951) was a general of the 1911 Revolution and one of the earliest Chinese Marxists, who joined the Communist Party in 1923 while holding a seat in parliament and a vice-ministership. His True Record of the 1911 Revolution in the North is a primary source for that upheaval.

ch01.anchor: Chen Duxiu was General Secretary
ch01.note: Chen Duxiu (1879–1942), a founder and the first General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party and a leading light of the New Culture Movement. Blamed for the catastrophe of 1927 and later expelled as a “Trotskyist,” he died out of favor.

ch01.anchor: a poem the late Ho Chi Minh, Chairman of the Vietnam Workers' Party, gave to Chen Geng
ch01.note: Ho Chi Minh (1890–1969), the Vietnamese revolutionary leader, had known Chen Geng in Canton in the 1920s; in 1950 Chen Geng served as a Chinese military adviser to the Viet Minh in the Border Campaign against the French. The couplet—“In the jumbled hills a lofty scholar lies; out of the deep dense woods a hero comes”—gives this section its title.

ch01.anchor: Chen Geng's years underground began with the failure of the Great Revolution.
ch01.note: The “Great Revolution” is the Chinese name for the Nationalist–Communist alliance and Northern Expedition of 1924–27. It “failed,” from the Communist standpoint, when Chiang Kai-shek turned on his allies in the coup of 12 April 1927 and the nationwide purge that followed—the White Terror this section recounts.

ch01.anchor: The "party purge" was a movement of reverse selection
ch01.note: The “party purge” (qingdang, “party purification”) was the Kuomintang’s violent expulsion of Communists and the left from its ranks, beginning in April 1927. The casualties the author cites—some 310,000 killed—are drawn from the Communist Party’s own Sixth Congress (1928) and run well above most independent estimates; they are best read as the Party’s own reckoning of its losses.

ch01.anchor: even Chen Lifu was sick at heart
ch01.note: Chen Lifu (1900–2001), with his brother Chen Guofu, led the “CC Clique” that controlled the Kuomintang’s party machine and its Zhongtong secret service. His memoir is quoted here against his own side.

ch01.anchor: the leaders of the "February Seventh" great strike
ch01.note: The railway workers’ strike on the Beijing–Hankou line was crushed by the warlord Wu Peifu on 7 February 1923; the union leaders Lin Xiangqian and Shi Yang were executed. It became a martyrs’ touchstone of the early labor movement.

ch01.anchor: the "August Seventh" Conference
ch01.note: The emergency conference of 7 August 1927, held secretly in Hankou, ended Chen Duxiu’s leadership, set the Party on the path of armed insurrection and land revolution, and raised Qu Qiubai to its head.

ch01.anchor: the arrest of Chen Yannian
ch01.note: Chen Yannian (1898–1927), eldest son of Chen Duxiu and secretary of the Party’s Jiangsu committee, was arrested and executed in Shanghai in 1927. Zhao Shiyan (1901–1927), named just after, was another leading organizer executed the same year; both are canonical martyrs.

ch01.anchor: Qu Qiubai presided over the enlarged meeting
ch01.note: Qu Qiubai (1899–1935), writer, critic, and Party leader who headed the Communist Party after the August 1927 conference. Captured by the Kuomintang, he was executed in 1935; his prison essay Superfluous Words has made him a contested figure ever since.

ch01.anchor: Li Qiang — a Special Branch veteran
ch01.note: Li Qiang (1905–1996) built the Party’s first clandestine radio transmitter and its early ciphers in Shanghai. After 1949 he served as Minister of Foreign Trade. His firsthand testimony, quoted at length here, is a principal source on the Special Branch’s origins—including his insistence that its true name was the “Special Branch,” not a “Special Affairs Bureau.”

ch01.anchor: the head of the Soviet advisory group, Borodin
ch01.note: Mikhail Borodin (1884–1951), the Comintern’s chief political adviser to Sun Yat-sen’s Kuomintang from 1923; when the alliance broke in July 1927 he left China through the northwest. He later perished in Stalin’s camps.

ch01.anchor: When the Wang Jingwei clique
ch01.note: Wang Jingwei (1883–1944), once Sun Yat-sen’s heir apparent and leader of the Kuomintang “left,” headed the Wuhan government that broke with the Communists in July 1927 (the “separation from the Communists”). He is chiefly remembered now for later heading a Japanese-sponsored puppet regime, 1940–44.

ch01.anchor: The man was Mei Baoji.
ch01.note: Mei Baoji (1881–1947), a veteran of the 1911 Wuchang Uprising and a Republican parliamentarian, is honored in Party accounts as the first intelligence source the Communists ever ran (from 1927, on Japan). The long biography that follows is the author’s defense of him as a man of principle rather than a paid informer.

ch01.anchor: on the night of 10 October took the viceroy's yamen
ch01.note: The Wuchang Uprising of 10 October 1911—still marked as “Double Ten,” the national day of the Republic of China—set off the revolution that ended the Qing dynasty. The accidental bomb blast in the Russian concession the day before, described just above, forced the rebels’ hand.

ch01.anchor: joined their names to form the "Chou'an Society,"
ch01.note: The Chou’an Society (“Society to Plan for Stability”), formed in 1915, was the pressure group—its “six gentlemen” led by Yang Du—that campaigned to make Yuan Shikai emperor. Among its lights were the translator and thinker Yan Fu and the classicist Liu Shipei, both named here.

ch01.anchor: Mei Baoji's nephew Mei Gongbin
ch01.note: Mei Gongbin (1901–1975) spent decades as a secret Communist buried inside the Kuomintang and the “third-force” democratic parties, helping to found the Revolutionary Committee of the Kuomintang. Arrested in 1955 in the Pan Hannian affair, he was cleared only after his death; his true Party membership was disclosed at his 1980 memorial.

ch01.anchor: our Party and the Nineteenth Route Army
ch01.note: The Nineteenth Route Army won fame for its stubborn defense of Shanghai against the Japanese in early 1932. In November 1933 its generals—Li Jishen, Chen Mingshu, Cai Tingkai and others—revolted against Chiang Kai-shek and set up a short-lived “People’s Government” in Fujian, the “Fujian Incident,” which collapsed within two months.

ch01.anchor: with Song Qingling elected honorary chair
ch01.note: Song Qingling (1893–1981), widow of Sun Yat-sen, was the most eminent left-leaning figure of the Republic and a protector of the Communist underground; she later served as a vice-chair, and honorary president, of the People’s Republic.

ch01.anchor: "The rain has passed, yet the fragrance lingers; such purity is not soon forgotten."
ch01.note: The couplet, by the Macau businessman and statesman Ma Man Kei (1919–2014), gives this section its title; its second line, gaojie zi nanwang—“such purity is not soon forgotten”—is the phrase rendered in the heading.

ch01.anchor: This was the "May Thirtieth" massacre
ch01.note: On 30 May 1925, British-officered police of the International Settlement fired on a student demonstration on Nanjing Road, killing about a dozen. The outrage set off the nationwide May Thirtieth Movement of strikes and boycotts—a decisive surge of Chinese anti-imperialism and a making of the early labor movement.

ch01.anchor: we stored the four at Shen Yanbing's home
ch01.note: Shen Yanbing (1896–1981) is far better known by his pen name, Mao Dun, the great novelist of Midnight. In these years he was an underground Communist, and—as here—lent his home to the Party’s work.

ch01.anchor: Yan Karlovich Berzin
ch01.note: Jan Berzin (1889–1938), a Latvian-born Bolshevik, headed Soviet military intelligence (the Fourth Department, later the GRU) from 1924 to 1935 and oversaw the Moscow training of Chinese agents, Gu Shunzhang and Chen Geng among them. He was shot in Stalin’s purges.

ch01.anchor: on the model of the Soviet State Political Directorate
ch01.note: The State Political Directorate (GPU/OGPU) was the Soviet political police and intelligence service, forerunner of the KGB; the Russian historian’s point is that the Special Branch’s counter-espionage committee was built to this model.

ch01.anchor: The man who "faced heaven and laughed, the blade at his own throat"
ch01.note: From the death-cell poem of Tan Sitong (1865–1898), the reformer beheaded after the failed Hundred Days’ Reform: “I face heaven and laugh, the blade at my throat; / I leave behind two hearts, bold as the peaks of Kunlun.” He is the archetype of the martyr who welcomes death for a cause.

ch01.anchor: "carries a twig in his beak to the end of time in a body but an inch long."
ch01.note: An allusion to the myth of the Jingwei bird: a drowned girl reborn as a small bird that carries twigs and pebbles forever, trying to fill the sea that killed her—the emblem of tireless, seemingly hopeless devotion.

ch01.anchor: *Qui nescit dissimulare, nescit vivere*
ch01.note: “He who does not know how to dissimulate does not know how to live”—a maxim of Renaissance statecraft long linked to Louis XI of France. Its sense supplies this chapter’s title, “No Concealment, No Survival.”

ch01.anchor: Li Dazhao and Fang Zhimin were such models
ch01.note: A roll of canonical Communist martyrs: Fang Zhimin (1899–1935), leader of the Jiangxi soviet, executed by the Kuomintang; Xiang Jingyu (1895–1928), the Party’s first woman Central Committee member, executed in Wuhan; and Jiang Zhuyun (1920–1949), “Sister Jiang,” tortured and killed in Chongqing on the eve of liberation and later mythologized in the novel Red Crag.
